narrative:
When your law school application was reviewed, a prediction model estimated that you had a 69 percent chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. This is considerably above the risk threshold the school uses, and that elevated risk was the reason your application was denied. The model does not use race or gender, but it does weigh academic signals heavily, and several of yours raised a clear red flag.

The single most influential factor was your class standing in your third year of undergraduate work. You ranked in the bottom tenth (decile one), while students who were accepted typically placed near the middle of their class in their third year. That is a dramatic gap, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure because it suggests persistent academic difficulty rather than a one-time stumble.

The second most important factor was your LSAT score. At 20, it was far below the average of roughly 37 for accepted students, and this reinforced the prediction toward failure. The model sees this as evidence that you may struggle with the reasoning-heavy demands of legal study and the bar exam.

Interestingly, the third factor, your family income background, actually nudged the prediction slightly in your favor. Coming from a lower-middle-income household was associated with a small positive influence toward passing, possibly reflecting perseverance or motivation. However, that small advantage was nowhere near strong enough to outweigh the two much larger academic concerns.

To improve your chances in the future, focus first on retaking the LSAT after serious preparation, and consider post-baccalaureate coursework or a structured academic program to demonstrate that you can perform at a higher level. Reapplying with stronger evidence of academic ability would give the next review a very different picture.
